On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture) the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Inspection and Sale Act, chapter 85 of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide: (1) that the Governor in Council, by regulation, may prescribe the kinds of imported fruit, the packages containing which must be branded or marked; the brands or marks to be used thereon; the manner and places in which such fruit is to be inspected and such packages branded or marked; (2) that all packages of fruit not branded or marked in accordance with such regulations shall be forfeited, and (3) that any person violating any regulation shall be liable to a fine of not more than $50 and costs.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

This amendment of the Fruit Marks Act relates to the inspection of fruit in the Northwest and all over the country as well. It is designed to put the Act in such a shape that we can place everybody, both the Canadian grower and his foreign competitor, on an equal basis. When the Act was first put on the statute-book, it was designed primarily for the export trade, not only for Nova Scotia, but for other parts of Canada that were exporting fruit. It is only in quite recent years that the tremendous competition from outside points into our country has been experienced; and, with the development of that competition, especially during the last year or two when it has been abnormally heavy, it has been found there was a weakness in the old Act, inasmuch as it was rather doubtful whether we had the power to deai in the case of the importer, with the branding and marking provided for under our

Act. Consequently, this resolution and the Bill to be founded upon it are designed to give to the department power to put everybody on an equal basis as regards the marking of the fruit. I might point out to the committee that during the last year or two there has been an enormous amount of fruit coming into all parts of the country, not only the prairie provinces but British Columbia and Ontario as well, through American channels, which is not graded and marked in accordance with our own Act. I think the Canadian grower who is kept up to the strict requirements of the Act feels that he is facing competition that does not put him on an absolutely fair basis; and this amendment will give power to the department, therefore to deal specifically with imported fruit, and thus remove a doubt which existed under the Act as to whether we had the legal power to deal with importations in the same way as with our own product.
I would ask the minister whether this legislation is in response to the request which was made to him by a delegation of fruit growers which waited on him two months or more ago.

It is in response practically to a demand which has been growing for many years, as I remember. Perhaps the hon. gentleman knows that fruit growing is my own special business, and so I am fairly familiar with conditions both East and West. During the last three or four years there have been repeated demands to have the Fruit Marks Act put in such a shape that it would place everybody on exactly the same basis. During this year there was an abnormal glut in our market of surplus fruit from the various producing districts of the western states and the situation got rather acute. We had not only a very large number of resolutions sent from all over the country, but we had before the Agricultural Committee an inquiry into this whole matter at which representative witnesses from Nova Scotia, from Ontario and from British Columbia-these being the three largest fruit-growing provinces-were sworn and gave evidence; and I think I speak quite accurately when I say that there was absolute unanimity of opinion and complete agreement in the evidence given. So, although it is true in a sense that this may be the result of the various delegations that have been down to Ottawa this year to give evidence before the committee, it is true also that it is the culmination of a large number of requests made during the last three or four years.

The reason I have asked is that I have reasonable grounds for believing that an application from the protected fruit-growing industry visited the minister and requested him
Mr. BURRELL.
to put an additional duty on fruit. He could not see his way to that, lest there should be an outcry on the prairies. The second best suggestion these fruit-growers from British Columbia had to- prefer to the minister was to ask that he at least take to himself power to make regulations which would be a very great handicap upon the coming of American fruit into Canada. The regulation, if one wnich the general interest of the country would require, would receive no opposition from me; but, representing a fruit consuming and fruit purchasing people, unless I receive further information on the subject, I am against it. I think this is merely-and I do not use the word in an offensive sense-an underhand way-I say again I do not use the word in an offensive sense-of giving to the fruit-growers of British Columbia the protection they seek against the competition, and I think the not unreasonable competition of the American fruit-grower. I have pretty good information that while the Government have flatly refused to grant an increase in the duty on fruit, because that would be so transparent and so flagrant, yet they practically promised this delegation that they would agree to their second request and change the administration and regulation in connection with the Fruit Marks Act. The measure here proposed will give to the minister the power to put what is in effect a tariff on fruit coming into the country from the United States.
No.
The minister is taking power to make regulations that there shall be certain marks put on the fruit boxes at the place of shipment.
Not necessarily.
The power is there.

My hon. friend will
pardon me; it is quite obvious that we would not have the power to impose upon a grower, for instance, in the Yakima valley, Washington, the duty of placing on his packages a certain mark. We cannot touch the growers on the other side of the line.

You can stop the trade.
I am surprised that the hon. minister, who is usually so fair, should give such a technical answer. I know that if a man does wrong in the State of Washington you cannot punish him in British Columbia or Saskatchewan.
' Mr. BURRELL: My hon. friend surely would not impose conditions which would dace the foreign competitor on anything Dut an equal footing with the home producer?

The question the minister put is no doubt a very plausible one,

but I am only a plain man, and I am not going to commit myself by giving a sweeping answer to such a question. I know that the hon. minister is a fruit grower, and no doubt, a reputable and independent one, but the fruit growers, I fear, have his ear to a greater extent than the grain growers have. The power the minister proposes to take under this resolution is one which he might exercise in a way that would have the very same effect as if the Finance Minister, in his Budget Speech, had announced his intention to place additional restrictions against the importation of fruit into this country. I am against giving to any person, even the hon. Minister of Agriculture, the power to create an additional difficulty and an added expense with regard to the bringing into this country of fruit for consumption by my constituents. The growers of apples in the States of Washington and Oregon are such large dealers and their market is so very extensive that they are not going to change the size of their boxes or go to any trouble with regard to putting special marks on them merely to obtain the benefits of the comparatively small market afforded to them in Canada. The truth of the matter is that when you effect restrictions either as to the size of the packages or the placing thereon of special marks, you are going to cause the United States shipper to refrain from shipping his goods into Canada as effectually as if you were to impose an additional duty. The original intention of this Act was that it should apply to foreign shipments out of Canada, and that there should be Government inspection of and control over the shipment of. fruit. Afterwards it was applied to fruit shipped between one part of our country and another. But if you make the men who are catering to the immense market of ninety millions in the United States conform to arbitrary legislation with regard to the size or stamping of the boxes, I am afraid that you are going to prejudice them to such an extent that they will not consider our market as being worth the trouble. Under the existing scale of duties, Canadian growers receive all the protection they ought to have. They get protection of thirteen and one-third cents a box on apples, and in addition they enjoy a differential freight and express rate amounting to almost fifteen cents a box, so that the total protection enjoyed by them in regard to apples is something like twenty-eight cents a box, which is forty per cent of the value of the apples f.o.b. This advantage in the freight rates applies to Alberta and Saskatchewan, and as the minister is aware, the province of British Columbia does not commence to supply all our demands. I regard this as a suspicious resolution, as something which is
brought forward to please political friends in that stronghold of Conservativism, British Columbia, where they love protection so much, and as something that will work out to their benefit and to the detriment of the consumers on the prairies. I know the minister would not do anything underhand, but I desire to warn him to be careful that he is not unconsciously made the instrument of those clever fruit growers in that province. I think the British Columbia dealers are getting on very well at present. If the consumers on the prairies do not kick very much, I think the British Columbia fruit growers should let sleeping dogs lie, and not send delegations to Ottawa asking for additional duties and for stricter regulations against the very small competition they have from the United Sates. I am very suspicious of this legislation, and if carried I predict that it will work out to the further protection of the orchard interests in British Columbia.

The wording of this
resolution is rather peculiar, and I would like to ask the minister what this means:
That the Governor in Council may prescribe the kinds of imported fruit.
I suppose that does not mean the Governor in Council may prescribe that certain kinds of fruit may not be imported into Canada?

Certainly not. It prescribes the kinds of imported fruit, the packages containing which must be branded or marked. Our Act, in its working out, is largely designed for the apple or standard fruit trade. There are many fruits that are not designed to be marked or branded in a special way, even under our Act. It is quite obvious that there are many fruits not grown in Canada, such as citrus fruits, that we would not touch at all. I was rather surprised at the tone of the criticism launched at this resolution by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles). I do not think this resolution or the Bill which is to follow will be found to be at all underhand, or, indeed, to be anything but most absolutely fair. My hon. friend has evidently given a little study to this matter, and he says he has grave suspicions that something very dark and nefarious lurks behind this Bill. If I was a lawyer, I would certainly have given a great deal of attention to matters of law, like my hon. friend, but, if he will allow me to say so, having been following one business for thirty years, I certainly have had to give a great deal of attention to that particular business in all its various details, and I can assure him that not only my business capacity, but also as Minister of Agriculture and as a representative of the people of British Columbia in this

House. I have given the fullest and fairest consideration to the whole matter. I shall not have time to go into it now; my hon. friend will readily admit on the second reading of the Bill there will be given a better opportunity to answer questions and thresh out matters in connection with the Bill. I would like to point out, however, that this Act is not designed to prevent the importation of fruit from the United States; far from it. My hon. friend has yet to meet, as I have, a British Columbia or Ontario or Nova Scotia fruit grower who does not cheerfully realize that it is up to him to meet competition from the United States or from any other country, and to meet it in the fullest and fairest way. My hon. friend seems to have the idea that under the new regulations we would have very extraordinary powers. The regulations are limited by the powers of the Act itself. We can only make them according to the spirit and letter of the Act itself. I frankly tell my hon. friend that I do not think he is speaking the mind of all his own people. I would point out to him that it is true that $150,000,000 of Canadian money is wrapped up in the fruit growing industry in Canada. In many lines of fruit people have to wait for, five, six or seven years before getting any return on their investment and surely that industry is at least deserving of fair encouragement by any government in this country. I think my hon. friend will admit that.
Certainly.

Let me add that the
growers have felt for years that they were entitled to more protection. My hon. friend has worked out the protection they receive in rather a larger measure than can be justified by the facts and certainly the growers have repeatedly urged requests for a raising of the tariff. I have frankly told my fruit growing friends that, notwithstanding any sympathy I might have in that regard, it was hopeless to expect the Government to deal at this session with any revision of the tariff except in one or two extraordinary cases such as the minister has dealt with and that I could certainly hold out no hope that they would get a raising of the tariff on fruit this session.
Not this session but there is hope for the future?

This session certainly. It is time enough to deal with future questions as they come up. I am not dealing with future question or expressing any opinions. I also pointed out that it might be difficult to get what they wanted this year, even in the face of a tremendous Mr. BURRELL.
dumping of American fruit which sometimes brought nothing to the American producers. The fruit men made a strong plea for the exercise of the dumping clause in our own legislative power but I pointed out the difficulty there, although I admitted the justice of their plea, for I could give many instances in which ten carloads or fifteen carloads sometimes came into this country in one day, not bought by importers but simply sent on consignment for anything it would fetch, even if it fetched nothing that would give a return to the producer himself. In many cases the big valleys of the western United States this year produced thousands of carloads of fruit and were overstocked in their own markets so that they did not get enough to pay for the freight and packing. Many thousands of trees in some of the western valleys were left simply unpicked. When those conditions existed there was fair justification for asking the exercise of our powers under the dumping Act but I said the difficulties were such that it was not possible to deal with it. They also urged the charging of an inspection fee. Although I had a strong sympathy with this suggestion, I had again to say that the Government thought it was better not to touch that and simply to confine ourselves to an Act which would make the American competitors come into the Canadian markets on an exact equality with the Canadian producer; and if my hon. friend has a word to say in opposition to a sentiment of that kind, he places himself in an extraordinary position. This Act is not designed only for the grower or for the importer of American canned fruits, it is also designed in the interest of the consumer. It is eminently propjer and right that the consumer when buying fruit should know that he is buying what the fruit purports to be from the marking of the package. I think everyone will agree that in that respect the Fruit Marks Act has been a benefit to the fruit consumers of Canada, and it has strengthened the proper packing and grading along all lines. He could not object to that. My hon. friend said, in regard to the tariff, that this was only increasing the difficulties of getting American fruit. I want to quote to him an authority from the prairies who says he represents the prairie farmers. I am quoting from a debate in this House not many years ago on the tarriff:
I speak for a class of people very far removed from the place where fruit is produced, and I regard it as a most artificial arrangement that we who live so far away from Niagara should be called upon to build up a trade there to an extent that is not re-sonable. We are not loath to pay a little duty and to do a little protecting when it is for the sake of our brother farmers. If it

were for any class of people other than those who are farmers like onrselves out there,
I would oppose this duty, even as it stands here to-night. We are giving a large protection for these people, hut I am free to say to the people whom I represent, and I often have to defend this fruit duty out there, that it is for the tillers of the soil that this item is there, and it is because of that that we are willing to accept the duty.
That was the language of Mr. Knowles, the hon. member for Regina in 1907. If he knew, as I know, the conditions of the thousands of men who for years have been putting into Their fruit investments every cent of capital they have; have for years waited patiently for results, and have developed the fruit industry under great hardships, he would sympathize with them when at last they met a condition of things where the American producer, who was flooded in his own markets, could come into the Canadian markets with brands absolutely misleading as far as the public is concerned, putting on his packages such marks that he could sell fruit that was often not better than, and sometimes inferior to, the British Columbia fruit, because the grower in British Columbia had To live up to the stringent requirements of an Act that the American compeTitor was not subjected to. I am sure that he would sympathize with that type of farmer and at least grant Mm that measure of justice which would give him a fair and even competition on his own ground. I assure my hon. friend and other gentlemen interested in this question in the West-and I know they are very much interested in seeing that their constituents, the consumers, get fair-play-that, as Minister of Agriculture, I am interested in seeing that the farmers of Canada get fair-play as well as the consumers, and this Bill is for nothing but to insure that when producers, whether they are American, Canadian or from anywhere else come into the Canadian markets they will all have to toe the same mark in catering for the consumers of Canada.
The minister has read some remarks which I made a good many years ago at the time of the tariff revision, in 1907 I think. That is a long time ago. Fruit has got high in the meantime.
That is longer than 1909.

Yes, longer than 1909. I still stand by that, I agree with what I said. All that I said was that if there must be protection that which is least distasteful to us is that which goes to our brother tillers of the soil. I do not believe in protection at all, I abhor it but if there is to be protection the place where we least welcome the attack on it will be against the
protection to the fruit growers, because they are farmers and are not organized and are of little strength. That is entirely different from giving consideration to the great incorporated trusts, monopolies and combines with which our friends opposite are on such close terms. The minister has said that the Washington fruit growers dumped their fruit, I presume he means into the prairie provinces. I am not going to set up as an expert in fruit with the minister, but I am credibly informed by men who give all their time to the fruit business, wholesale fruit buyers, as large as there are in western Canada, I am informed by two of them that they have obtained information from shippers in the State of Washington, that they get the best price for all the shipments into the Canadian markets, after they pay the duty and that there is nothing in the way of dumping, simply getting the best price. I have here a letter, the signer of which I shall not disclose, but I will make his sentiments my sentiments as I have absolute confidence in what he says. He writes:
I am advised that the British Columbia, growers complain that the American shippers have been dumping their fruit into the Canadian market, that is selling it for less money on this side than in their own markets. I have letters from the managers of three of the largest associations in Washington and in each case they state that on Canadian markets they obtain better prices for their fruit than in any state in the Union, and from personal knowledge I know that to be the case.
I dismiss that dumping business as just a kind of blanket charge because the fruit growers who want more protection know the weakness of their case and they make that charge that we cannot disprove. Under the machinery of the law they have the opportunity to prove it and they have the Minister of Agriculture to help them into the bargain. In any event, if they do dump it, I wish they would dump more. If the minister lived on the prairies he would wish that more people were around leaving strawberries or apples or any fruit at his door. The complaint I make is that they are not dumping enough.

I did not pretend to
argue on that question. I dismissed it as having nothing to do with the resolution.
The minister will agree that we are equally transgressors.

I was simply saying
that we had not acceded to it.

My complaint is that
the fruit growers to-day have far the better end of the stick and they should be satisfied with what they have. We are afraid of this legislation and if the fruit growers are not satisfied they will stir the

people up so that they will agitate against the existing duty. The Minister ot Agriculture says that he owns trait orchards in British Columbia.
I did not say anything about it.

He said he was interested in the fruit business, and I assumed he was an owner. I thought I was fair in saying that he owned it when he said he was in the fruit business in British Columbia, and if the minister is in the fruit business in British Columbia, I think I am safe in saying that the minister's fruit farm has in the last six or seven years been multiplied in value all the way from five to ten times.
Why?

Because the fruit growers of British Columbia have had the market of the prairie consumers. More than that, it is the prairie men who have gone out to British Columbia and have spent their money in buying land there that has caused the fruit lands of British Columbia to become extremely valuable. We on the prairies have made their fruit land valuable and then the fruit growers come back with the argument that because they have stocked up their orchards with trees and increased their plants and because their land has become so valuable, we must pay more for our fruit. Because they have been able to find a very profitable market on the prairies their land has gone up in value and then they say to us: Our land has become so valuable, that you must give us a great big percentage of profit. In some instances the land is worth fifty times what it was from five to eight years ago. If the land has gone up in value so rapidly, it is evidence that it must be a profitable business. The fruit growers must make enormous profits if their plants have multiplied in value from five to ten times in the course of as many years. They ought to be satisfied with that and not try to use that as an argument for making increased profits at the expense of the consumers upon the prairies. We welcome their fruit in our country, but I will say this: Let the fruit growers be satisfied to find on the prairies a profitable market for their product and do not let them try to make us a mark because there is a limit to what we will stand from them.

I agree largely with what the hon. member for Moose)aw (Mr. Knowles) has said in regard to this matter. I believe that the intentions of the hon. the Minister of Agriculture are good, but at the same time I live close to the province of British Columbia, and I know something about the comparative prices of fruit. The fruit growers in Washington have now an entrance into Mr KNOWLES.
that part of the country, and American fruit is the lever in fixing a fair price, which can be used against the British Columbia fruit grower to a great extent. I look upon this amendment as permitting the possibility of obstacles being placed in the way of the entrance of American fruit at the present rate of duty into the province of Alberta. I am in sympathy with the British Columbia fruit grower. I would like to see British Columbia fruit used entirely on the prairies, if it can compete on a fair basis with the fruit from Washington. I believe that British Columbia has not taken advantage of the opportunities on the prairies by organizing properly to dispose of its fruit. The Washington growers look after the business of the prairies, the wholesalers handle their fruit very freely, and they get it in packed to the satisfaction of the consumer. The complaint I have heard against British Columbia frequently is that the fruit growers _ there have not an organization on the prairies to handle their fruit and to see that it arrives on the market in good shape and properly packed. They look upon the people of the prairies as being convenient to them. The people on the prairies are only too glad to purchase British Columbia fruit, but not at a premium over American fruit. We should not have any obstacles placed in the way of this American fruit coming into Alberta. I do not know where the minister intends to place these inspectors, but with regard to fruit coming from Washington, I presume that the inspectors would be stationed at some point in the state of Washington, or at the points of entry into British Columbia and Alberta. The fruit may be interfered with on its way into these provinces by officials who are anxious to protect and assist the British Columbia fruit growers. They might be over officious in that way. If the British Columbia fruit grower can develop the trade of the prairies, and if he can ship his fruit into Alberta and Saskatchewan, and sell it at as cheap a price as the American fruit can be placed on the market, and if it is a good grade of fruit, I would much prefer seeing British Columbia fruit used entirely on the prairies. But, as the minister knows, Washington fruit is used largely at the present time in face of the duty that exists and in competition with British Columbia fruit. Unquestionably, British Columbia fruit is good, but the British Columbia growers should organize a better system of disposing of their fruit on the prairies than that which they have at the present time. It would be a great injustice to the consumers of fruit o,n the prairie if obstacles were placed in the way of the entrance of competitive fruit. There is also the question of freight and express rates with which British Columbia fruit growers have to con-

tend, but these difficulties ought to be overcome and the fruit growers ought to be able to arrange for proper transportation facilities so that they will be able to reach the large centres of consumption upon the prairies and place their fruit on the market there in a condition and at a price to successfully compete with American fruit.

I would like to ask the minister if the intention of the Bill is to make the foreign shipper conform with the same regulations as the Canadian shipper has to conform with and if the marks are all the same.
Yes.

Will the minister see
that the department notifies the foreign shippers of these regulations so that their fruit will not be subject to confiscation?

Undoubtedly; we have no other wish at all. As a matter of fact, they have been supposed to comply with the regulations, but it has been impossible to make them comply altogether with the marks that the Act prescribes. I would like to say, in answer to what has been said by the hon. member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) and the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) that there is a little mistake about the way in which this matter has been taken up by the hon. member for Moosejaw. After all, this Act is only designed to make the Canadian producer live up to certain standard of packing, grading and marking when he ships to England or anywhere in this country. The consumer then knows exactly what he is getting because the marks and brands are provided for, and all the Act does is to make everyone else who is catering to the Canadian consumer simply live up to the spirit and the letter of the Act in Canada, to which the Canadian producer has to live up.	.

One objection to this is that it is apt to lead to vexatious regulations with regard to the importation of American fruit. From the evidence I have heard in the Agricultural Committee this session, it would appear that the agitation for an Act of this kind is coming from British Columbia. The Washington shippers have been shipping a great deal of fruit into western Canada, particularly into Alberta, and these gentlemen from British Columbia were crude enough to suggest to the committee that vexatious delays should be placed against the importation of American fruit coming into this country. I would point out to the minister that the wording of the resolution places a great deal of power in the hands of the minister or any official of the department. The port of entry at which the inspection shall be made might '

admit of a great deal of difficulty on the part of the importers of American fruit if the officials of the Government were not very careful to give due consideration to the matter. We on the prairies depend a great deal at present on American fruit, and probably seventy-five per cent of the apple shipments to Alberta come from the United States. I have no reason to say that these apples as they are shipped are not up to the standard. The reason for changing the Marks Act cannot be to improve the grade of the fruit very materially, because on the evidence brought out at the Agricultural Committee there was no objection particularly taken to the grade of fruit shipped by the Washington shippers into Alberta. I think the minister should be very careful in introducing this measure to see that no discrimination ot vexatious delay should accrue to importers of American apples into Alberta.

That is not true.
Well, have these values grown.
They have grown.

The value of western
lands has greatly increased ?
The values have increased considerably, but the farmers of the West do not want any protection. They are not afraid of anybody in competition.

I am not speaking of
that; I am asking if the value of western lands has grown very greatly or if this boom which we hear so much about is all nonsense.

The Western lands
have increased in value extremely.
Let me ask the hon. member if the farmers of the West want the whole business; do they want everything ?

I would answer my
hon. friend briefly; if we were all getting to be millionaires in the West, what does that matter; we still have our rights. Have not the manufacturers in Toronto increased their wealth and built their clubs and mansions, and whoever heard of us writing to them and saying we want so much on every bushel of wheat out of all the money you are making. We might

make that demand with much better grace, because they are making the money out of us; we are not making it out of them. Parliament must lay down the underlying principle. Look at the widespread classification of freight that the railways have drawn up themselves and
imposed on this country. It is almost impossible now to have that classification simplified in the interests of the shipper, and Parliament ought to put in the Railway Act a principle supporting the idea of simple classification. The commission is growing in size, growing in numbers, growing in salaries, growing in the number of lawyers that are retained, and I am told that the lawyers for the railway companies are coming to the hearing of this case with big trunkfuls of briefs and evidence which has not been digested, and which, if it is digested, cannot be handled in a satisfactory way by the Railway Commission. My protest may be feeble, I am speaking only for myself, but I say the conviction that is growing on the people of Canada is that the railway grievances in their substantial form must be approached in Parliament, and relief must come immediately from Parliament if it is to be effective. Relief is not in sight to-day, and I have not seen anybody who can give a satisfactory reason to the people of Canada why this discrimination in railway charges should prevail against the West in favour of the East; nor can anybody tell me now that that enormously rich corporation, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, should not forthwith reduce their rates. I believe they are willing to do so if a way can be found to make them do it. If that concession involves some temporary and unfair discrimination against the other two roads, then Parliament may find a way of compensation. The Railway Commission cannot find the method of compensation; they cannot devise the policy necessary to meet the case. Therefore, while I admit the ability of the Chairman and the good services which he has rendered to the commission, that commission have made no substantial headway in dealing with the great question of the inequality of rates, of simplifying the classification of rates, and are not in a position to define a policy that ought to underly railway charges in this country, because the charges are not split up into state charges as they are in the States, with more or less state jurisdiction over them. Parliament has unlimited power; it has delegated that power to the commission, but the policy has not been delegated. We can never get a commission, po matter how much energy they display, to come to a conclusion in favour of equality in rates. The West is entitled to equal freight rates and, by reason of that overflowing treasury, of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, to that reduction which we were promised years ago and to which we are entitled, as I believe and have always contended, according to the original charter of the Canadian Pacific Railway

Company. I again direct the attention of the Minister of Railways and the Government to the fact that the relief that the West calls for will not come from the commission but from some kind of action by this House, led by the Minister af Railways, by amendments to the Railway Act.

I am pleased to see that the Government are recognizing the important services of the Chairman of the Railway Commission by incrasing his salary in accordance with the responsibility of his position. I am only sorry that the great services of Mr. Justice Mabee were not recognized in a similar fashion. We have a capable man at the head of the Railway Commission, and I think he deserves this increase.
I would be very sorry to see the question of freight rates dragged into this House and wrangled out here. No time would be saved by any such experiment. I can imagine a committee of this House listening for weeks and months to trunkfuls of evidence and trying to fathom this very intricate question. I do not agree with my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean). I think the question is in the proper hands, and I have no doubt that the commission will satisfy the people of the country in their findings, as soon as it is possible for them to complete their labours. They have a great many questions constantly before them. I presume in time, as the importance of the Railway Commission increases, as it must, owing to the increased prosperity of the country, that tire other members of the commission will also be recognized.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, as a farmer and as representing the county of Lapraire-Napierville, entirely inhabited by a farming community, I wish to enter a protest, in their name, against this resolution asking that the salary of the chairman of the Railway Commission be increased from $10,000 to $12,500 per annum. The first reason of my opposition is that the highest salary paid, in this country, to a public officer, that is to the chief justice of the Supreme Court, is but $10,000, and the fact that the Prime Minister himself gets but $12,000. I fail to see why the chairman of the Railway Commission should get a higher salary than the Prime Minister or the chief justice of the Supreme Court.
I may add that there are other members of that commission who get $8,000 each, per annum.
If the hon. Minister of Railways is still the head of that department next year, he will, perhaps, apply for an increase in behalf of the other four commis-Mr. W. P. MACLEAN (South York).
sioners who, I think, are already well paid. By the way, I may say that the Government is always desirous of favouring the big fellows. We have, in the civil service, many employees who get modest salaries, varying from one thousand to twelve or fifteen hundred dollars per annum, men who have families to bring up, as those high grade officers have, and nevertheless, nobody ever talks of an increase in their behalf, whereas we are increasing by $2,500, at one stroke, the salary of just one man whom we have recently appointed chairman of the commission. This is doing an injustice to all the other employees of the country. For that reason, I am against the resolution now before you, Mr. Chairman, and I propose:
That $12,500 be struck out of the resolution and $10,000 be inserted in place thereof.

In reply to my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), I know that the commission appointed by my predecessor have for some time been investigating the question of telephone and telegraph lines and have not yet reported. I have endeavoured to bring this investigation to a close so as to give effect to whatever finding the commission may make. They will report very soon in reference to western freight rates. When discussing this subject here the other day, a number of hon. members felt that a case had been made, showing inequality of rates in the West. There is no doubt about that. The Chairman of the Commission tells me there are 230,000 different tariff rates to be considered. Anyone who thinks of that will shudder at the idea of this House trying to go through and to adjust this enormous number of rates. It may seem that they have been investigating this question for a long time, but I feel that, in order to go through all this detail and to get the rates on an equal basis, the commission are not taking too long. I am quite safe in saying that within a couple of months they will bring in a ruling in reference to the question of rates.
In reference to the amendment of the hon. member (Mr. Lanctot), the fact that the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court does not get more than $10,000 is no reason why the members of the Railway Commission, which comes so closely into contact with the public, should not be well paid. I feel that our Supreme Court judges do not get enough. That does not come under my department. I hope the time will come when the Supreme Court judges will be better paid, because we cannot expect in a young country like this, to get good men capable of filling these very important positions unless we are prepared to give them a decent living. And, as the cost of living, which is so much talked about in this

country has gone up, what was good enough for this position ten years ago, $10,000 a year, is not equal to that now. I cannot accept the amendment of the hon. gentleman.

May I ask the minister if any arrangement has been made or is being made that a superannuation allowance shall be granted to the retiring members of the Railway Commission? I understand that these men were appointed for ten years, subject to re-appointment. And some of the members are getting old, and when their time expires, they will not be looking for re-appointment. I would like to know if the minister has decided upon any superannuation for retiring members of the commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know whether
the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Buchanan) is aware, but special provision was made in the case of two gentlemen who filled the position of chairman of the commission. Mr. Justice Killam, and Mr. Justice Mabee were both gentlemen who had been on the Bench for some years. When they were appointed to the position of chairmen to the Railway Commission, special provision was made that their service as chairmen should count in respect of their superannuation. They had partially earned their superannuation as judges, but their service as chairmen of the commission was to count. That, roughly speaking, was the effect of the arrangement. Outside of that there has never been any provision for superannuation allowance for the members of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada.

The Prime Minister replying to the hon. member for Medicine Hat gave some information as to two gentlemen who had been taken from the Bench to become chairmen of the Board of Railway Commissioners. But that is not all that the hon. gentleman asked
No superannuation allowance has been made for any others.

I understand that. But 1 think the hon. member for Medicine Hat was asking if the Government were considering any plan to provide superannuation for these gentlemen. Take, for instance, the present chairman; he was not taken from the Bench, but was taken from his practice which he had to give up, and separating himself from that practice for ten years, will break up his connection. And the other members of the commission are in the same position. I would like to know whether the Government have anything in view to make provision for that.
I was asking also in regard to members of the Board of Railway Commissioners who are retiring within a few years at the expiry of their term of appointment, ten years.
No provision made for them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is no provision
under the law at present, except in the case to which I have alluded, and I have always understood that the two gentlemen whom I mentioned declined to accept the chairmanship of the commission except on a provision of that kind. There has been no such arrangement made for the new Chairman, nor, I think could there have been an arrangement of that kind entered into, because he had not been a member of the Judicial Bench. It is perfectly true as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Buchanan), has mentioned, that appointment to the Board of Railway Commissioners does not carry with it an opportunity for a retiring allowance as does an appointment to the Bench. It is also perfectly true that unless the Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners of Canada is taken from the Judicial Bench as a man of experience and ability must be selected, it is usually true that he must give up a very much larger income than even that provided by the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways. These are matters for consideration. My hon. friend from Humboldt (Mr. Neely), has asked whether the Government has any announcement to make on the subject. At the present time, I cannot say the Government has reached any conclusion on the subject, nor has there been very much opportunity to consider it, but we will not forget what the hon. gentleman has suggested in that regard, and later we may have an opportunity to give it more consideration than it has had up to this time. However, I do not want to be understood as committing the Government to the proposal that there shall be a superannuation or an allowance. The subject has not been considered and we are not in a position to make an announcement now.

I am inclined to think that it would be difficult to get a first class man as Chairman of the Board of Railway Commissioners, a position which does not carry with it any superannuation allowance, for a salary less than the salary proposed, $12,500. But I think the Government ought to consider the salaries of all the judicial or semi-judicial positions with a view to having something like an equality in those salaries. It seems somewhat absurd for a man in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia or Prince Edward Island, a chief justice, and these gentlemen like some of the puisne judges, are men of great ability, to be given only $7,000 a year, while a gentleman holding the position of Chairman of the Railway Commission, presumably of no greater ability than some of these others, receives nearly double the salary. There is an anomaly also in the

members of the International Waterways Commission. That is a tribunal which ought to be, if it is filled toy good men who separate themselves entirely from the ordinary political and legal work, ought to command the respect of the people of both countries and ought to be one of the most valuable tribunals ever created in any country to settle questions arising between two countries. These gentlemen receive $7,500. But I understand they are allowed to practise their profession. One
fentleman I know, a very important mem-er of the commission may be hearing an important international case to-day and to-morrow may be carrying on a case in the county court. I do say that not only does that detract from the standing of the International Waterways Court, but it enables a member of that court who receives $7,500 to earn a great deal more from his professional work, making his income double that of a Supreme Court judge. It is always discouraging to a judge of the highest court to find a gentleman occupying a judicial position appointed to a tribunal of no great importance getting a greater salary than a judge of the highest court in the country receives. I think there should be some effort to arrive at an equality in the salaries in order to do justice to the gentlemen occupying these high positions, and so that the best men can be obtained. So far as the resolution is concerned, I for one am inclined to think the amount is not too large.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will no doubt appreciate the fact that the members of the commission, to whom he has alluded, are appointed for a period which may not exceed five years, and in addition to that, 'the position does not carry superannuation. The course which was adopted with regard to the three gentlemen appointed was, I think, that laid down by the late Government.

I do not think there was any Order in Council passed on the subject. When the matter came before me I informed one of the gentlemen at all events, Mr. Barnhill, that he would be expected to devote all his time to the work.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I speak subject to correction, but I am certainly under the impression that I found some record of the then Prime Minister's statement that they would not be debarred from practicing. I quite agree that I do not recollect any Order in Council to that effect, but I think that was the policy as I understood it.

Perhaps I might refresh my right hon. friend's memory. I think he will find a letter from Sir George Gib-Mr. PUGSLEY.
bons in which he stated that he preferred being employed by the day. The Order in Council passed by the late Government, however, provided for an annual salary of $7,500.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not remember that. I have a distinct recollection-unless I am greatly mistaken-of a letter from Sir Wilfrid Laurier to the effect that I have just mentioned.

Possibly there may have been.
Amendment (Mr. Lanctot) negatived.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time and concurred in.
Mr. COCHRANE thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 200, to amend the Railway Act.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.
On the order being called for the consideration of Bill No. 21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire, as amended in Committee of the Whole-Mr. Borden:

I rise to object to this Bill being taken into consideration at the present time. I would like to call my right hon. friend's attention to the fact that he gave the right hon. leader of the Opposition a memorandum of certain bills that would come up for consideration at this sitting. When the leader of the Opposition informed me that it would not toe convenient for him to be here, he called my attention to the list handed to him by the Prime Minister, and this Bill was not among them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Was the right hon. gentleman under the impression that this Bill would not come up?
I am satisfied he must have been.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Then we will not go on.

On motion of Mr. Borden, the House went into Committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Conservation Act, and to provide for the appointment of an officer as assistant to the Chairman and secretary to the Commission, who shall have the rank and salary of a deputy head of a department.
(Mr. Deputy Speaker in the Chair.)

This does not increase
the number of salaried officials?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No. It lias been suggested that instead of appointing a secretary, one of the present officials mi^ht foe appointed as assistant to the Chairman and secretary to the Commission, with a view to his discharging as a permanent official, some of the duties now assumed by the Chairman, and doing more useful and effective work than he has been able to do under the present system. The Bill ,as proposed to be introduced has been commended to my consideration by Mr. Sifton, the Chairman of the Commission. I consulted him and Mr. White, the secretary, before deciding to bring this measure before the House. Mr. Sifton is thoroughly of the opinion that more effective work could foe done if this measure were passed and if the 'staff of the Commission were reorganized to that extent.

The appointment of a
deputy head will mean the addition of one official?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It does not mean the
addition of an official; it means that one of
the officials Who is now employed by the commission will receive a different status
and a slightly increased salary. It is not the intention to appoint any additional officials-at least no such intention has been communicated to me.
Resolution reported, read the first and the second time and concurred in.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.	.

For fear my right hon. friend may misunderstand me about item number 6, I have spoken to the chief whip on our side. While it is true that the leader of the Opposition showed me on the Order Paper to day my right hon. friend's reference and number 6 was not included, yet the chief whip of this side siays that there was no agreement that it would not be taken up. I think it only right to mention that to my right hon. friend, so that he will understand that that is the position.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the absence of the
right hon. leader of the Opposition, and in view of the objection raised by my hon. friend, I would not proceed without his consent. I am perfectly ready to proceed, and would prefer to do so, but I do not want to be understood as taking the slightest advantage of the absence of the leader of the Opposition.

The difficulty is that the
chief whip of this side told the chief
whip of the Conservative side that we would be willing to go on. I am perfectly willing to waive my objection in view of that understanding.

It is only Tight to say, so far as any agreement is concerned, the Government are at perfect liberty to proceed with number 6, and I think the chief whip of the Government will bear me out in this. There was some talk at six o'clock, and I distinctly stated that if the Government saw fit to proceed with the measure, so far as we were concerned, we would be quite willing to proceed. I make that statement so that there may be no misunderstanding whatever.
On the order being called for the consideration of Bill No. 21, to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire, as amended in Committee of the Whole-Mr. Borden:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That the said Bill, as amended, be now considered.
Mr. PUGSLEY, in amendment, moved:
That Bill 21, entitled 1 an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective Naval Forces of the Empire,' be not now considered, but that the same be referred back to a Committee of the Whole House for the purpose of considering an amendment proposed thereto by Mr. Carroll, the member for South Cape Breton, and likewise for the purpose of having the said Bill, with any amendment or amendments, regularly and properly reported to the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not consider this amendment in order. It seems to me it should set out that the Bill he amended in some special direction, and if necessary give "the proposed amendment. It does not do so; it says: 'an amendment proposed by Mr. Carroll.'

The reason why I make my motion is that the report of the committee has not yet been received by the House, is not properly before the House, and not properly on the Order Paper. You have only to look at ' Hansard ' to ascertain that. As a matter of fact, when the chairman of the_ committee handed yon the Bill you put the question to the House: when shall the report be received? and immediately my right hon. friend the Prime Minister moved the adjournment of the House, so that no order was passed by the House for the reception of the report, and therefore it is not in a position to be taken into consideration. That is one ground. I would call Your Honour's attention to page 9827 of ' Hansard.' This is what took place. After some discussion with regard to the report of the committee,

which I felt it my duty to allege was not in accordance with the facts, I said:
Mr. Pugsley: The Chairman made a false report to you.	.	,
Mr. Speaker:	When shall this report he
received ?
That is the question Your Honour put. Some hon. meinbers cried out: 'No, don t receive it.' My right hon. friend then moved immediately the adjournment of the House. That is the statement in Hansard.' Mr. Borden moved the adjournment of the House. Then the question was put, and Your Honour declared the motion for adjournment carried, so that the report is not properly upon the Order Paper.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When the question was asked, I immediately followed it by stating :	' At the next sitting of the House.
I remember stating that because I was not aware whether it was the desire to consider it at that sitting or at the next sitting of the House, and the clerk reminded me of the order, and I left it at that. I think it would be in order to move that the report be not now considered, but that the Bill be referred back for further consideration; but I do not think that the proposed amendment is regular ot that it would be in ordeT.
Would Your Honour allow me to discuss that briefly?
No.

I was addressing myself to His Honour the Speaker. I do not think it is quite in order or in keeping with the dignity of the House for any gentleman, when the Speaker is appealed to, to call out and in that way intimate what the Speaker should do. When a gentleman says no, that is rather a reflection upon the Speaker I was appealing to His Honour the Speaker as the impartial presiding officer of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I remember very distinctly, and I can refer to the clerk, who came up and spoke to me about it, as I said I was not aware whether it was desired to proceed with the consideration at that sitting: The rule says:
All amendments made in committee are reported by the Chairman to the House, which shall receive the same forthwith. After report the Bill is open to debate and amendment, before it is. ordered for a third readin". But when a Bill is reported without amendment, it is forthwith ordered to be read a third time at such time as may be appointed by the House.

Of course, I cannot dispute Your Honour's word and if Your Honour feels sure that you have a recollection of it, I would not. All I can say is that I did not hear you, and certainly Mr. PUGSLEY.
' Hansard ' did not and I doubt if any hon. member heard you.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I am quite sure that
the House must have heard me, and I can appeal to the clerk, who stood beside me. I was not aware whether it was the desire to deal with it then or at a future time, and he reminded me that it must be at the next sitting of the House. I repeated that quite loudly.

To be accurate, I
might say, Mr. Speaker, that there is nothing in ' Hansard ' beyond what I have said. There is another reason why I claim that the amendment should not be considered to-night, and it is this-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would like to understand where we are. If the hon. member is speaking on this motion, of course, he could not do so, because I have held that it is not in order. But if he makes the motion that the Bill be referred back for further consideration, he will be in order and can speak on it.

With Your Honour's
permission I will change the motion.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have the Votes and
Proceedings before me, and they say that:
' The Bill was reported with an amendment, to be considered at the next sitting of the House.'

We are in this position, that it does not appear to have been accepted according to ' Hansard. The Votes and Proceedings say that it was. They are made up afterwards by the clerk. Your Honour's recollection is that it was. Then, I beg to move:
That Bill No. 21, an Act to authorize measures for increasing the effective naval forces of the Empire, be not now considered but that the same be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House for further consideration.
In support of this motion I would like to call Your Honour's attention to the fact that, before the report was submitted to Your Honour, there were two motions before the committee. One was an amendment by my hon. friend from South Cape Breton (Mr. Carroll) to the effect that Canadian materials should be used, in so far as practicable, in the construction of the vessels provided for by the Bill. The Chairman refused to allow the member for South Cape Breton to place that amendment before the committee. I submit that it was illegal and irregular for him to refuse. I am sure you will see the importance of it because, if the Chairman was right, then all that the Government has to do is to postpone from one day to another the various clauses of a Bill, then take advantage

of the opportunity immediately to rise, move that the committee report the Bill and in that way absolutely prevent any member of the House from moving an additional section, or additional sections, to the Bill. The effect of making a motion that further consideration of different sections be postponed and that they shall be the first business considered upon the date to which the consideration is postponed, prevents the consideration of any additional sections which may be proposed until the clauses, the consideration of which has been postponed, have been disposed of. Therefore, it absolutely prevents any private members of the House from suggesting any additional sections for the consideration of the committee. The Chairman held that the hon. member for South Cape Breton should not have the opportunity of putting that amendment. Now, I submit that he was clearly wrong. But further, Sir, when he was about putting the motion that the Bill be reported, I moved that the Chairman leave the Chair. That is a very important motion. If it had carried it would have superseded the motion of the right hon. the Prime Minister and would have left the matter open for my hon. friend from South Cape Breton, or for any other hon. member to again seek to claim the Chairman's ear for the purpose of proposing an additional section. It clearly appears upon ' Hansard ' that the motion was put and 1 desire to say upon mv responsibility as a member of this House that the Chairman undoubtedly heard the motion, because he actually put the motion to the committee and immediately afterwards changed it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I think the hon. member is now getting upon ground which would have_ to be approached in another way. Bourinot, at page 280, says, in reference to the Chair:
If a member wishes to challenge his action or conduct, he must proceed in the usual way, by giving notice of a motion on the subject.
Therefore, if the aim of the hon. member is to deal with the Chairman's conduct, it would not be permissible for him to do it in that way. It would be necessary for him to move a substantive motion after giving the usual notice.

I am not challenging
the conduct or motives of the Chairman. I am not reflecting upon his motives.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: But the hon. gentleman is challenging his action, and that is the same thing. The action of the Chairman cdnnot be discussed in this irregular way.

The motion which Your Honour Tefers to is a .notion the obiect of
which would be to censure the Chairman. But, my motion goes farther than that; my motion goes to the foundation of the report to Your Honour.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The rule says:	'If a
member wishes to challenge his action.' If that is not challenging the Chairman's action I do not know what plain English means and therefore it would be improper. I think the hon. member would be quite in order to make the motion which he proposes and to support that without challenging the conduct of the Chair.

Well, I will simply
state the facts for Your Honour as I understand that is what Your Honour means. A motion, a3 I have said, was made that the Chairman leave the Chair. That motion was made under rule 15 which has not been altered by the resolution that was passed by a majority of the House. Rule 15 is as follows:
A motion that the Chairman leave the Chair, is always in order, and shall take precedence of any other motion.
My contention is that that motion having
been moved, as appears by ' Hansard ' and, as I stated, on my responsibility as a member of this House, it was the duty of the Chairman, under the rules, to have put it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I call the hon. member to order, because he is violating in the same way the principle that I have already twice referred to. The hon. member is quite in order to move that the Bill be referred back; but I am quite sure that he is not in order when doing that in questioning either the motives or the action of the Chairman. That can only be done in the proper way.
How can I get it back unless I show Your Honour there has been an irregularity and illegality in the proceedings?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: A Bill may be referred back many times without giving any special reason other than that it is the desire to amend it in some direction by adding a clause or in some other way. It is a very common practice to refer a Bill back, and it does not require that it should be made the occasion of a reflection on the regularity of the conduct of the Chairman or the propriety of his action. There was a proposed amendment read by the hon. member (Mr. Carroll) which it would be quite competent to read again, and to give it as a reason why it is desired to refer the Bill back.

Do I understand Your Honour to say that as a reason for referring the Bill back I cannot show that the

Chairman acted contrary to the rules of the House, and that in the case of a motion which supersedes another motion, he illegally and improperly ignored it?
Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I think the hon.
gentleman is too old a parliamentarian to speak in that way; he is giving a very ba.d example to younger members. The rule is so plain and so easily understood that it should be conformed to.

I can remember a time when judges used to almost commit lawyers for contempt of court because they challenged the decisions of the court, but in modem days that idea is regarded as barbarous. Every lawyer has to-day the right to criticise judgments and to show error in these judgments, and surely in this age-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I have given my ruling on this point, and if the hon. member (Mr. Pugsley) is not satisfied, he can appeal to the House. But, I must insist on maintaining the rules of the House.

Mr. Speaker, my experience in the past has shown me there is not much use appealing to the House. I understand that Yout Honour refuses to allow me to show that the Chairman ignored the motion that he leave the Chair. Is that Your Honour's ruling?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
My ruling is that an
hon. member cannot reflect on the Chair or call in question the action of the Chair, except in the regular way.

There is a belief in the
minds of a large number of the members in this House that the Chairman did not properly report this Bill.
Order.

That belief being in their minds and the Bill therefore not being properly before the House in its present stage, I would ask Your Honour what remedy is the House to have, believing that its rules have been broken?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The remedy is to give
notice of a motion to call in question the conduct of the Chair, and then the House, if it so wills, can rectify its own conduct in such way as it sees fit. That is the remedy and the proper one.

But if the Bill has
passed.

I think all of us on this side of the House wish to draw a distinction between the passage of the Bill according to the rules of the House, and any question there may be in regard to the propriety of the action of the Chairman. The two matters are in our minds distinct. We Mr. PUGSLEY.
are prepared, if it is necessary, to challenge the action of the Chairman, but the main point is to nave a thorough understanding as to what the rules of the House-mean, and what their effect is, as illustrated by this concrete case, and we want to know then if it is Your Honour's ruling that this Bill is properly before the House and if it is not we want to have the procedure taken that will put it before the House properly.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is to my mind the
easiest thing in the world to make a motion to refer the Bill back. If that is agreed to, the Bill will be before the committee as it was, and then a remedy can be had if it is regarded as not having been properly reported to the House. So far as I know, in my judgment, it is properly reported to the House. That is so far as I know, but I was not cognizant of everything that took place. But if there is anything to rectify, the thing to do is to refer the Bill back and put it in the position it was in before.

That is the point. We are not anxious to refer it back for the purpose of amendment; we are anxious to refer it back because it is improperly in its present stage before the House, and in order to give reasons why it should be referred back we have to give a statement as to how it comes to be in its present stage, without desiring to reflect upon any person's action.

Let me clearly understand. Your Honour will see that in order to ask to have the Bill referred back we have to convince the majority of this House that it should be referred back; and what better way can you point out in which we can induce the majority so to believe than to show if I can that the chairman had illegally reported the Bill. I am sure the House then would feel it its duty to rectify the error of the chairman.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: In doing that, the hon. member must see that he is reflecting directly on the Chair, and the rule says that cannot be done in that way.

If I may again trespass- I am aware that I am trespassing, but I do it with your permission, Mr. Speaker- if it is the belief of a large minority of the members of this House that the rules which are on the order book for the purpose of regulating the business of the House, in the protection of the lights of the minority as well as in the assertion of the rights of the majority- if they believe, I say, that these rules have been violated, and if they can show properly and plainly that they have been violated, is there no remedy within the rules of the House ?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: There is a remedy by doing as I have suggested from the first, namely, to put a notice on the paper and discuss it until the House reaches a conclusion as to what is right to be done in the premises. That is the proper remedy.

very root of the rights of the House. We should have the point settled before it is applied to this particular Bill. 1 take it that it is the desire of everybody that having rules we shall have the benefit of them, either assisting us in our views or protecting us in our rights. The other night, Mr. Speaker, you appealed to us for order, for the maintenance of the prerogatives of the House and for the support of the rules. Every person, who has the responsibility of representing the people of this country in Parliament, must be desirous of having the business of the House carried on with due decoroum and due respect to the rules; but we must have the belief that the rules are properly interpreted, or we cannot be expected to give to the rulings that respect that is absolutely necessary.

I understand that the
motion to refer back the Bill to committee does not necessarily mean a reflection on the Chair. We are simply asking to have it referred back, because in our judgment an error in procedure was rpade. I would like to have your Honour's opinion on this.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I do not understand the hon. member. I see no difficulty in discussing the motion to refer the Bill back, but I do see strong grounds against reflecting upon the conduct of the Chair, or discussing the conduct of the Chair without giving due notice and putting it in proper form. The other day an hon. member, when the Chairman had made a ruling, said that the leader of the Government had not the floor. No one but the Chairman has the Tight to say who has the floor. The only way in which his ruling can be challenged, if two members get up at the same time, is to move that the other member has the floor. the Prime Minister having moved that we report an amendment cannot be moved.
So, you will see that the hon. member for St. John has good cause to move that this Bill be referred to the Committee of the Whole for further consideration. And while I am on this point, I would like to know from you under what rule the motion has to be made to report a Bill from the Com mittee of the Whole. I have been in this House for a great many years, and I have attended the consideration of numberless Bills in Committee of the Whole, and I have always noticed that after all the clauses had been considered the Chairman, as a measure of precaution, says, 'Shall I report the Bill?' We all understood that question as having been put in view of the fact that some hon. member had wished to add a clause to the Bill. I do not see how he could ignore that fact, because I well remember that the right hon. gentleman was present when the hon. member for South Cape Breton attempted to move that clause. But be that as it may, he moved, to report the Bill, and then Mr. Carroll moved to add a clause, and the right to move that motion was denied to the hon. member.
